mods.prompt:
Build me a Claude Code mod called "switchboard": a pane that lists every Claude Code session on this machine and tells me which one is waiting on me.

How sessions find each other: each session running the mod writes one small JSON file about itself to ~/.claude/switchboard/<session id>.json (under CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR when set): its name, its state, where it runs (terminal, desktop or nothing attached), what a dialog waits on, when that state began, when it last had a turn, a heartbeat time, and its cost so far when Claude Code reports one. Never any message text. It rewrites the file when its state changes and every 30 seconds; a file not rewritten for 90 seconds means the session is closed.

The name: the title in the desktop sidebar (a custom-title line in the session's transcript), else the one Claude Code writes (ai-title), else the folder. Read it with `tail -c 262144` on the session's own transcript when it starts and at most every two minutes at a turn's end, keeping only the title lines.

States, from the session's own events: working (a turn started), needs you (Claude Code's own "waiting on you" notification; say what for: "a permission for Bash" from the tool the turn last called, "a question", "a plan to approve"), error (the turn ended on an error), idle (the turn ended), closed (inferred from a stale file). After a dialog is answered and its tool runs, it is working again. A /clear marks the old conversation gone and carries on under the new id.

What I see
- /switchboard opens a pane: "N need you" in amber (or "Nothing needs you" in green), then "You are here: <name> (<where>)", then one row per session, who needs me first: a mark and a colour per state (! waiting, ✕ error, ● working, ○ idle, - closed, never colour alone), the name, the state in words ("waiting on a permission for Bash · 2m", "idle for 9m", "closed 2m ago"), where it runs, and the cost when it is a cent or more.
- Idle sessions with no turn in the last hour fold into one line ("26 quiet sessions") with a Show button. Closed ones sit dimmed at the bottom.
- While another session needs me: one line above my prompt saying which and where, with Show, and a count in the footer ("1 needs you"). Never for this session's own dialog.
- A toast the moment another session starts needing me, once per change, never on the first read, saying where it is.

Rules
- Read the other files every 5 seconds only while I am looking at this session, the newest 60 at most, and only the files that changed; redraw only when what is on screen changed.
- Watch only: never focus, answer or type into another session. No network, no model calls; the only command it runs is that tail.
- Clean every name to one line with no control characters. Skip half-written or unknown files.
- Terminal and desktop app. Other mods' lines above the prompt come first.

Tests: this session's own record through its events, the title from a transcript tail, the pane, band and footer from fake sessions in every state, the quiet fold, exactly one toast per change, no redraw on unchanged reads, and every file touched inside the switchboard folder.

```
    waiting on a permission for Bash · 2m
✕ tests           stopped on an error 5m ago             terminal
● docs            working for 2m                          terminal   ≈$0.49
○ web             idle for 12m                            terminal
○ 26 quiet sessions: idle, no turn in the last hour       [Show]
- old             closed 2m ago                           terminal
```

## Install

```
/plugin install switchboard --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

Install it in every session you run (a user-scope install does that): each session shows up once Switchboard runs in it.

## Use it

- **`/switchboard`** opens the pane. The first line says how many sessions need you, and the next one says which session you are in and where.
- **One row per session**, who needs you first: a mark and a colour for its state, its name (the title in the desktop sidebar, or the one Claude Code gives it, else its folder), what it is doing in words, where it runs, and its cost so far when Claude Code keeps that figure.
  - `!` **waiting on** a permission (and for which tool), a subagent's permission, a question, a plan to approve, or an answer
  - `✕` **stopped on an error**
  - `●` **working**
  - `○` **idle** (or **new**, opened and not prompted yet)
  - `-` **closed** (it stopped reporting; listed for an hour)
- **Quiet sessions** (idle, with no turn in the last hour) fold into one line. **Show** unfolds them; each new start of the session folds them again.
- A session waiting on you says what for on a line of its own. On a narrow pane the names shorten first, so the state and where always show.
- **While another session needs you**, a line above your prompt says which and where (`! Fix the login needs you (desktop)`, with **Show** to open the pane), and the footer counts them (`1 needs you`). Never for this session's own dialog, which is already in front of you.
- **A toast** the moment another session starts needing you, once per change: `Fix the login needs you (desktop).`

It only watches. It never switches to, answers or types into another session: go to that session to answer it.

## Settings

- **On:** on by default. Off, Switchboard writes no record, reads no other session's and draws no line, footer count or rows; switched off while it runs, its record says closed one last time, so other sessions stop showing this one working or waiting on you. `/switchboard` says it is off. `/config` or the modmyclaude hub flips it, live.

## What it can touch

- **Writes:** one small file for this session, `~/.claude/switchboard/<session id>.json` (or under `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` when that is set), rewritten when its state changes and every 30 seconds, and once more, as closed, when you switch Switchboard off. It holds the session's name, state, where it runs, what a dialog waits on (a tool's name, such as `Bash`), three times (when its state began, when it last had a turn, and when the file was written), whether it is new (not prompted yet), and its cost figure. The name is the session's title, which Claude Code writes as a short summary of your first prompt (or you set in the desktop sidebar), else the folder's name. Nothing else of your prompts, Claude's replies or your files.
- **Reads:** the other files in that folder, every 5 seconds while you are looking at this session (a terminal or the desktop app attached) and whenever this session's own state or title changes, only the ones that changed since the last read. Its own session's events: turns starting and ending, the tool a turn calls, Claude Code's own "waiting on you" notice, the session title, and the cost figure.
- **Runs:** `tail` on this session's own transcript (its last 256 KB) to find the session's title: when it starts, and at a turn's end at most every two minutes. Until the session has a title it also looks at every turn's end, at Claude Code's "waiting on you" notice, at a /clear or resume, and at the first prompt, so a new session gets its name quickly. Only the title lines are kept; the rest is never stored or shown.
- **Session state:** the rows as last read, and whether the quiet ones are unfolded.
- **Network, model calls:** none.

## Limits

- A session shows up only once Switchboard runs in it. Sessions started before you installed it appear after their next restart, or at once where Claude Code hot-loads the mod into them.
- A dialog shows as waiting about six seconds after it opens, when Claude Code raises its own notice; once you answer it, the row says working again after the tool it asked about has run.
- A closed session is inferred: one that has not rewritten its file for 90 seconds is shown as closed. A computer waking from sleep shows its sessions as closed for up to half a minute.
- A brand-new session shows its folder's name until Claude Code titles it, usually after the first prompt. On a host with no `tail` (Windows), the title comes only with your next prompt.
- Files of old sessions stay in the folder (a few hundred bytes each): Claude Code gives mods no way to delete a file. They are never read once older than an hour, and you can delete the folder at any time.
- Two sessions with the same name get the first characters of their ids to tell them apart.
- An older session that has had no turn since Switchboard loaded into it counts as quiet, since its last turn is unknown.
- The pane, the line and the footer are checked through the engine's test kit on the terminal and desktop surfaces.

## Built from a prompt

This mod was built from [the Switchboard prompt](../../prompts/switchboard.md).

# Thermostat

Shows when your prompt cache goes cold, and stops the expensive send.

Claude Code keeps your conversation in a prompt cache. After a stretch of quiet (about an hour on a subscription, 5 minutes on an API key) the cache lapses, and the next message re-reads the whole conversation at the full cache-write price. Thermostat shows you that clock, holds the surprise send once, and can keep the cache warm while you are away when that is actually cheaper.

## Install

```
/plugin install thermostat --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

**The countdown.** At the end of the prompt footer, beside the mode labels:

- `cache warm · 41m left` - quiet while there is time
- `cache warm · 8m left` - amber in the last 10 minutes (the last 2 of a 5-minute window)
- `cache cold · 182k to re-read` - once it has lapsed
- `· warming 1h12m` is added while `/warm` runs

This draws on the terminal and the desktop app. Where no footer draws (VS Code, mobile, or a footer that is hidden) the same text appears on the plain status line under the prompt, without colour. Nothing shows until the conversation has something cached.

**The guard.** When you send a prompt on a cold cache, it is held once and you see what it costs:

> Cache went cold 23m ago: this send re-reads 150k tokens (~$1.20 vs ~$0.03 warm, Opus 5.5 API list prices).
> Send again to go ahead, or /clear to start fresh.

Send it again to go ahead (the words are put back in the prompt box if it is empty), or `/clear` to start a fresh conversation instead. It only holds prompts you type yourself (at the terminal, in the desktop app, or through Remote Control; never a headless `claude -p` run, where nobody would see the hold), only when the re-read is at least 20k tokens, never a prompt typed while a turn is running, and a hold counts as seen for 10 minutes.

**Keep-warm.** `/warm 90m` (or `2h`, `1h30m`, `45`) sends a tiny ping just before the cache would go cold, for as long as you asked. Before every ping it compares what the remaining pings will cost with what one cold re-read would add; if pinging costs more, it stops and says so in the transcript. It also refuses up front when the whole window would not pay. `/warm` on its own shows where it stands, `/warm off` stops it. Only a `/warm` you type starts or stops it; another plugin's command cannot. Confirmations appear as a toast; when it will not start, the reason stays in the transcript as a dim note. A window can run up to 24 hours.

How a ping works: it re-sends the conversation's last request (same model, system prompt, tools and messages) with one line asking for the word "ok", tools denied. That reads the conversation's own cache entry, which restarts its timer. Nothing is added to your transcript. Every ping's usage is checked: if it did not read the conversation back from the cache, keep-warm stops rather than keep paying for pings that are not helping.

**The receipt.** `/thermostat` opens a pane (a transcript note where no pane can be drawn, as in `claude -p`) laid out to the collection's UI standard: the cache right now as one line in its colour (`Warm · 41m left`, `Cold · 98k to re-read`), the window's bar and the next send's price beneath, Bolt beside them (asleep while the cache is cold or empty); then a row each, the figure at the right edge and the detail dim beneath, for cold sends paid (and how much more than warm they cost), prompts held (and how many you answered with `/clear`), keep-warm pings (what they cost, and the sends that arrived warm because of them), money saved, Claude Code's own estimate of the session's total cost (what `/cost` sums at list or managed prices, not your bill), and the guard; a figure still at zero draws no row. One footnote says what the dollars are.

## Settings

Every setting has a default, so the notice at install about options not yet set is expected; change them in `/config`.

| Field | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `guard` | `hold` | `hold` stops the first cold send once and shows the cost. `warn` shows the cost in a toast and sends. `off` does nothing. |
| `cacheMinutes` | `0` | The cache window in minutes, used until Claude Code reports its own. `0` works it out from your login. |

The window is worked out in this order: what Claude Code itself reports (its cache TTL on a model switch, or whether a resumed cache has expired), then `cacheMinutes`, then your login (60 minutes on a subscription, 5 on an API key), and 5 minutes when none of these is known.

Prices come from a small table of API list prices per model family (October 2026), with cache writes at 1.25x input for the 5-minute window and 2x for the hour. When Claude Code prices a re-cache itself (on a resume or a model switch, including an organisation's managed pricing), its rate is used instead. On a subscription the dollars measure how much of your plan a send uses, not a bill.

## What it can touch

- **Reads:** each prompt as you submit it (to decide whether to hold it; the text is not kept), the token counts of each main-conversation model request, what Claude Code reports on a resume or model switch, the prompt box (only to check it is empty before putting a held prompt back), which kind of login the session uses (the kind only: the credential stays with Claude Code, and this mod makes no network requests that could use it), and Claude Code's estimate of the session's cost.
- **Writes:** its own session state, the prompt box (a held prompt's words, only into an empty box), the footer label and status line, the receipt pane, toasts, and short dim notes in the transcript. None of these is sent to the model: `/warm` and `/thermostat` answer with no command output when you type them, so they cost no tokens. The only command text is a one-line notice when `/warm` is run by something other than you (keep-warm changes only with a `/warm` you type) and a one-line error notice if either command fails; neither carries any of your data. No files, no settings, nothing kept across sessions.
- **Processes and network:** none.
- **Model calls:** only keep-warm pings, only after you run `/warm`, at most one per cache window (about every 58 minutes on a subscription, every 4 minutes on a 5-minute window). Each costs roughly one cache read of the conversation plus a few tokens; the smart rule stops them as soon as they would cost more than they save, a window ends after 24 hours at most, and three failed pings in a row end it too.

## Limits

- The window is a model of the cache, not a reading of it. Claude Code only states its cache TTL on a model switch (and implies it on a resume), so until then it comes from your login or `cacheMinutes`. Other things can make a send cold early (tools or instructions changing, the cache being evicted); the receipt still books those from the real token counts.
- The countdown starts with the first model request after the mod loads, or with a resume. Installed in the middle of a conversation, it shows nothing until your next message.
- After a model switch the new model starts with nothing cached, so that first send is neither held nor counted as a cold send.
- A ping can make the model think, which is billed as output; the measured cost of each ping feeds the next decision. Pings cannot go out while the computer sleeps; if it sleeps past the expiry, keep-warm stops and says so.
- In the desktop app the held prompt may not go back into the prompt box (the app can refuse that); send it again from your history. The desktop app is recognised by its prompts arriving as an SDK host's with a desktop surface attached; prompts from the VS Code extension are not held.
- The guard puts a held prompt's words back into the prompt box (only when the box is empty); attached files are not put back.
- The footer label is checked through the engine's test kit on the terminal and desktop surfaces; how each terminal paints it has not been checked by hand.
- Prices are list prices unless Claude Code priced a re-cache itself. Amazon Bedrock and Google Vertex AI bill separately.

## Built from a prompt

This mod was built from [the Thermostat prompt](../../prompts/thermostat.md).

# Umpire

Runs your tests after Claude edits code and makes the call: passed and failed counts above the prompt, a toast when it flips. Off by default.

```
umpire: 142 passed · 2 failed · auth.test.ts, user.test.ts · 8.3 s
```

## Install

```
/plugin install umpire --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

Type `/umpire on`. From then on, at the end of every turn in which Claude changed files with its own tools (Edit, Write, NotebookEdit), umpire runs your project's tests once, and:

- **A line above the prompt** makes the call: passed and failed counts, the first three failing tests or files (`+2 more` past that) and how long it took, in the error colour when something fails. While the tests run it says so.
- **A toast** only when the call flips: the tests started failing, or they pass again. Never on every run.
- **The status line** keeps the count: `tests 142/144`.
- **`/umpire show`** opens the last run: the call, a mark per run for the last ten, the failing names, and the end of the output. **tell Claude** puts the failing names and the output's last 30 lines in your prompt box, after anything you typed, with anything that looks like a secret redacted. You decide whether to send it.
- **A hold** when a file that says what the tests run changes: `package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `pytest.ini`, `go.mod` or `Cargo.toml`. Claude editing one anywhere in the project, or anything changing one at the project root (a shell command, you), stops the runs that start on their own, and the line says which file. They wait until you start a run with `/umpire run` or **run again**, so a test command Claude just changed waits for you to start it.

It finds the test command once per session: your setting, else the one you set for this project with `/umpire command`, else `package.json`'s test script (through pnpm, yarn, bun or npm, by lockfile), pytest, `go test ./...` or `cargo test`. It understands the summaries of Jest, Vitest, pytest, go test and cargo test; for anything else, the exit code makes the call.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/umpire on` | Run the tests after each turn that changes files (only when you type it) |
| `/umpire off` | Stop |
| `/umpire run` | Run them now (only when you type it) |
| `/umpire show` | The last run, in a pane |
| `/umpire command <cmd>` | Set this project's test command, as you would type it (only when you type it) |
| `/umpire tell` | Put the failures in your prompt box (only when you type it) |

"Only when you type it" means typed by you in the terminal, the desktop app or Remote Control. A program you run that drives Claude Code through its SDK counts as you too, since the desktop app sends that way; another mod, a peer session or Claude running the command is refused.

## Settings

Every setting has a default, so the notice at install about options not yet set is expected; change them in `/config`.

- **On:** on by default. Off, Umpire runs nothing and draws nothing, and every `/umpire` command says it is off; switched on again, `/umpire on` (or the setting below) decides, as before. `/config` or the modmyclaude hub flips it, live. It runs commands, so another mod cannot switch it on; anyone can switch it off.
- **On from the start:** run in every session without `/umpire on`. Off by default.
- **Test command:** the command to run, as you would type it. Empty: found from the project.
- **Time limit (seconds):** 120 by default; a longer run is stopped and called timed out.

## What it can touch

- **Runs:** the one test command, in the project root, with `CI=1` and colour off so test runners do not wait in watch mode, stopped at the time limit. A command you typed (the setting or `/umpire command`) runs through `sh` as you wrote it. Nothing else.
- **Reads:** the project's `package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `pytest.ini`, `go.mod` and `Cargo.toml`, and whether a lockfile or `tests/` exists, to find the command and to see when one of those files changes. The paths of the files Claude's tools edit, to hold the runs when one of them is such a file.
- **Keeps:** the last ten runs' output, a million characters at most, in the mod's memory only. The command you set per project in its own store, keyed by a hash of the project's path.
- **Writes:** its session state (on or off, the runs' calls, the hold), the line, the status line, toasts, and your prompt box when you press tell Claude, never sent.
- **Network, model calls:** none of its own. Your tests may do anything your tests do.

## Limits

- Changes a shell command made (a formatter, a codegen script) do not trigger a run; only Claude's own file tools do. `/umpire run` covers the rest.
- One run at a time: a turn that ends during a run queues exactly one more, run when the first is done.
- Counts come from the test runner's summary line; go test without `-v` names failing tests but counts no passes.
- The run's output is shown as the runner printed it, without colour. Long output keeps its end. Past 4 MB the engine stops keeping it: the call then says `output cut at 4 MB` and may have no counts.
- The hold covers the files that say what the command runs. The tests themselves are code, and Claude may have written them: umpire runs them as your test runner would, so turn it on only where you would run the tests yourself. A command you set that reads another file (a Makefile) is not held when that file changes.
- The line, the pane and the presses are checked through the engine's test kit on the terminal and desktop surfaces, with the test runner stood in for.

## Built from a prompt

This mod was built from [the Umpire prompt](../../prompts/umpire.md).

# Wardrobe

Restyle Claude Code live, including colourblind-safe and high-contrast themes.

## Install

```
/plugin install wardrobe --marketplace modmyclaude/claude-code-mods
```

## Use it

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/wear` | Opens the gallery: a card per theme with a sample tool row drawn in that theme, its diff chips, Bolt in the theme's costume and a `wear` button; the one you wear is marked. Close it with its close mark or ctrl+x x. |
| `/wear <theme>` | Switches now. Rows still live on screen redraw in the new look, and the switch band shows the theme above the prompt for six seconds. |
| `/wear auto` | A day theme by day and a night theme by night (see Settings). |
| `/wear season` | The seasonal pack the calendar calls for, re-checked daily (see Seasonal packs). |
| `/wear pin` | This project keeps what it wears now; other projects keep the global choice. While pinned, `/wear <theme>` changes this project's pin. |
| `/wear unpin` | This project follows the global choice again. |
| `/wear <theme> --match` | Wears the theme and sets Claude Code's own `theme` setting (the `/theme` menu) to the built-in nearest it: a light look on a dark theme turns the theme light, keeping a daltonized or ansi variant. Your own theme is remembered. From the desktop app this changes the terminal's theme; the app keeps its own look. |
| `/wear match` | The same for the theme worn now. The gallery's `match theme` button does both at once. |
| `/wear default` | Back to Claude Code's own drawing. After a match, Claude Code's theme goes back to the one you had, unless you changed it yourself since the match: then your choice stands. |

Each command answers in a toast (an unknown theme's message stays longer). Nothing `/wear` says is added to the conversation, so it costs no tokens and never reaches the model.

Themes: `noir`, `paper` (light), `tokyo-night`, `dracula`, `catppuccin`, `solarized`, `nord`, `high-contrast`, `colorblind`, and the seasonal packs `halloween`, `christmas`, `spring` (light), `summer`, `autumn`. Short forms work too: `drac`, `hc`, `colourblind`, `tokyo night`, `xmas`, `fall`, `spooky`, and any prefix that names one theme alone (`sp` is spring, `su` is summer).

Every look also ships as a Claude Code theme file (`themes/<look>.json`), listed in `/theme` as "<Look> (wardrobe)". `--match` prefers it, so in the terminal the input box border, your message background, the text and the diff colours follow the look too; the desktop app keeps its own theme.

What changes, on the terminal and in the desktop app:

| Where | What wardrobe draws |
| --- | --- |
| Tool rows | A one-cell stripe in the theme's accent, the theme's icon for the kind of tool (shell, read, edit, write, search, web, agent, todo, MCP), Claude Code's own row, then a status glyph and, for a finished call, the time since Claude asked for it (any wait for your approval included). |
| Folded tool groups | The stripe, one icon per call before the count line; a failed call in the error colour. |
| Diff cards (Edit, Write) | Numbered lines in the theme's add and remove colours, with a `+N -N` summary. |
| Small shell output | A themed card; stderr lines are marked `!`, not only coloured. |
| Spinner | The theme's suffix after the word (never over Claude Code's own status message); on a terminal 60 columns or wider, a chip saying what the turn is doing (thinking, writing, using tools). |
| Turn duration | A themed `Baked for 3s` line (the terminal draws this line; the desktop has its own footer). |
| Above the prompt | The switch band, for six seconds after `/wear` (see below). |

### Seasonal packs

Five themes made for a time of year, each with its own mark and icons: `halloween` (pumpkin orange, violet and bone white on near-black, mark `☾`), `christmas` (holly green, berry red, snow white and gold on deep pine, `❄`), `spring` (a light theme: fresh green, blossom pink and sky blue on cream, `❀`), `summer` (sun yellow, sea teal and coral on deep navy, `☼`) and `autumn` (amber, rust, moss and cream on dark brown, `❧`). Every pair they paint meets the same 4.5:1 bar as the other themes.

`/wear season` picks one by the local date and is stored like `auto`: wardrobe re-checks the calendar once a minute, so the pack turns over at midnight on its own, and `/wear` names what it wears now and why.

| Dates | Wears |
| --- | --- |
| Oct 15 to Nov 1 | `halloween` |
| Dec 1 to Jan 6 | `christmas` |
| Jan 7 to the end of Feb | `nord` (the frost theme; the rest of winter has no pack of its own) |
| Mar 1 to May 31 | `spring` |
| Jun 1 to Aug 31 | `summer` |
| Sep 1 to Nov 30, Halloween aside | `autumn` |

### Bolt in costume

Bolt, the modmyclaude mascot, wears each theme: in the gallery beside every card, beside the line that names what is worn, and in the switch band. A costume is an accessory drawn over the sprite, never a change to it: a witch hat for `halloween`, a santa hat for `christmas`, a flower crown for `spring`, sunglasses for `summer`, a beanie for `autumn`, a cape and fangs for `dracula`, cat ears for `catppuccin`, a headband for `tokyo-night`, a fedora for `noir`, reading glasses for `paper`, a sun visor for `solarized`, a beanie with a pom for `nord`, a bow tie for `high-contrast`; `colorblind` leaves Bolt plain. Every costume takes at most three colours, all from the theme's own palette, keeps the antenna light clear (each hat has a notch around it), and never uses Bolt's own pink or blush. `tests/costume.test.ts` holds every one of those rules for every theme and pose.

### The switch band

For six seconds after `/wear <theme>` (and after `/wear auto` or `/wear season` resolves to a theme) a band above the prompt shows the switch: one row filled with the theme's background, carrying its mark, `wearing <theme>`, its five icons, and Bolt in the theme's costume at the right when the band is 60 columns or wider. It draws under any other mod's band, never while a survey holds the band, and goes away by itself. `/wear default` raises none.

### Accessibility

- `high-contrast`: every colour pair wardrobe paints is at least 7:1 (WCAG AAA).
- `colorblind`: added lines are blue and removed lines orange, never red and green; tool icons differ by shape (triangle, disc, diamond, square, cross, bars).
- Every other theme, the seasonal packs included: at least 4.5:1 (WCAG AA). `tests/themes.test.ts` checks every pair of every theme.
- Every theme gives each tool kind and each status its own glyph, so colour is never the only cue.
- Every coloured span is painted on the theme's own background, so the contrast holds whatever your terminal's background is.

## Settings

Every setting has a default, so the notice at install about options not yet set is expected. Set these in `/config`. A time wardrobe cannot read falls back to its default, and `/wear` names it.

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dayTheme` | `paper` | What `/wear auto` wears by day. |
| `nightTheme` | `tokyo-night` | What `/wear auto` wears by night. |
| `dayStarts` | `07:00` | When the day starts, 24-hour local time. |
| `nightStarts` | `19:00` | When the night starts. A day that crosses midnight (`20:00` to `06:00`) works. |

## What it can touch

- Its own store: the global choice, the per-project pins (keyed by the path of the folder the session started in), and, once you have matched a theme, the Claude Code theme you had before and the one it set, so `/wear default` can put yours back and can tell when you changed it since.
- For the session, in memory: each tool call's start and end time, for its row.
- Reads the project root, the attached surfaces, the clock, and Claude Code's own theme setting (the `/config` theme row) at session start, before a match and before a restore; it also notices when you change that setting.
- Writes Claude Code's theme setting only when you ask: `/wear <look> --match`, `/wear match` and the `match theme` button set it, and `/wear default` sets it back to the one you had. No files, no processes, no network, no model calls. It never refuses or changes a tool call: its tool hook only notes when a call starts and ends.

### What a look changes, and what it cannot

**It changes:** tool rows and folded groups, diff cards and small shell output, the spinner's word and suffix, the turn line, the switch band, your prompt rows, Claude's reply rows and command output rows (a stripe, and the look's background where it may paint), the `wearing <look>` label in the prompt footer, the `/wear` gallery, and, only when you ask with `--match` or the `match theme` button, Claude Code's own theme: in the terminal the input box border, your message background, the text and the diff colours then follow the look.

**It cannot change:** the desktop app's window frame, sidebar, input box, page background and fonts; Claude Code's own text colours inside the rows, which follow `/theme` unless you match it; the spinner's word, which keeps Claude Code's own colour; permission dialogs, errors, diffs over the size limits and long shell output, which Claude Code draws itself; the terminal emulator's background and font; VS Code and the mobile app; rows already printed on the terminal's main screen; and a light look's panels on a dark app, which stay stripe-only until the theme is matched.

## Limits

- It restyles what Claude Code lets a mod draw. Claude Code's own text keeps its colours: the tool's own row inside wardrobe's stripe, icon and status, Read and Grep results, the prompt, dialogs and the transcript all follow Claude Code's own `/theme`. Wardrobe styles around them (the stripe, the chips, the band, the gallery); pick a matching `/theme` for the same reading everywhere.
- Tool rows wrap Claude Code's own row instead of replacing it, so expanding a row and its output keep working.
- Claude Code draws these itself: errors, diffs over 120 lines or 8,000 characters, binary diffs, edits held for review, and shell output over 8 lines or holding a control character other than a colour code (a progress bar's carriage return, a bell, NUL).
- Untrusted text it draws (paths, diff lines, shell output, settings) is cleaned first: colour codes are dropped and any other control character shows as U+FFFD, since Claude Code refuses a drawing that holds one.
- Where another mod draws its own tool result or turn line, wardrobe steps aside and that drawing stands. Tool rows, tool groups and the spinner wrap whatever is beneath them.
- A pin belongs to the folder the session started in: a subfolder or a worktree of the same repo is pinned separately.
- On the terminal's main screen, rows already printed keep their look; new rows, and everything in the fullscreen view, follow `/wear`.
- VS Code and the mobile app are not restyled; `/wear` says so when one is attached.
- Where nothing draws a toast or a pane (a `claude -p` run), `/wear` writes its words and the list to the log instead.
- Auto mode and season mode check the clock once a minute, so a switch can land up to a minute late. A choice made in another session reaches this one the same way.
- The switch band is a plain row above the prompt: it never covers a safety hold or a survey, and Bolt is left out of it under 60 columns.
- Tool calls made before wardrobe loaded show no time, and a refused or failed call shows its status but no time.
- Not verified: the paint itself in a real terminal and in the desktop app. The tests check the drawn trees against each surface's rules, not pixels.

starters.name: mod-maker
starters.title: Mod Maker
starters.tagline: Describe the feature you wish Claude Code had. Get a tested, installable mod.
starters.prompt:
Build me a Claude Code mod: [what you want to see or change, e.g. "a pomodoro timer in the status line that chimes when 25 minutes are up and asks if I want a break"].

How to build it
- Mods are new (Claude Code 2.1.287+). Use your plugin-authoring skill and read the types it points to before writing anything.
- Pick the right shape and tell me in one line which and why: a band above the prompt, a side pane, a status line entry, a toast, a sound, a slash command, or a hook on tool calls or prompts.
- Keep it small: only draw and do what I asked. No network calls, no model calls and no reading files it does not need, unless I ask for them.
- If it can block or change anything (a tool call, a prompt), make it fail safe: when the mod itself breaks, it should say so, not silently let things through or silently block me.

Prove it works
- Write tests for the main behaviour, including the UI on both the terminal and the desktop app if it draws anything.
- Run `claude plugin validate` and `claude plugin test` until both pass.

Then
- Load it in this session so I can try it, and take my changes in plain words.
- When I say it is good: copy it to a folder I keep, install it so it loads in every session, and tell me where it lives and how to turn it off.
- Finally, add a marketplace file so I can share it, and give me the one-line install command to send a friend.

starters.title: Mod Matchmaker
starters.tagline: Let Claude check your setup and pick the mods worth installing, in order.
starters.prompt:
Read the mod catalogue at https://github.com/modmyclaude/claude-code-mods (the README and the prompts folder), then help me pick the mods worth installing.

Check my setup yourself first
- My OS, my Claude Code version (mods need 2.1.287 or newer), whether I am in a terminal or the desktop app, my terminal width, and whether my terminal can show images. Ask me only about what you cannot check.

Then ask me three quick questions
- Do I use subagents? Do I run long sessions or step away mid-session? Do I share my screen or record demos?

Recommend
- A table: mod, yes / maybe / skip, and one line on why for my setup. Flag anything that will not run here.
- Group the yeses into packs: Safety, Cost, Visibility, Looks. Order them by what I would feel first.
- Give the exact install line for each pick.
- Suggest one custom mod idea tailored to how I work, and offer to build it with the Mod Maker prompt.

Rules
- Do not install anything until I say yes to each one. Mods run with my permissions.
